title: Obon, the fifth time
hookLine: welcoming ancestors, and those you've lost these five years
tomorrow: the woman who raised him wove him a cloth. why give it away?

lines: RED FOR LIVING, WHITE FOR GONE.
cards: A plate of fruit beside an old photo, a small fire at the door at dusk: at Obon in Japan, families light welcome fires so the dead can find their way back to the old house. They come home.
At Vu Lan, a Vietnamese festival from the same root, something odder can happen at the temple door. At some temples, someone pins a rose on your shirt. A red one if your mother is living.
A white one if she has died. A festival of the dead, and red roses for the living. Why?

teach.b: Both festivals come from the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture. The first half is the part people retell. Moggallana finds his mother among the hungry ghosts, starving.
The food he brings her bursts into flame before she can eat it.

The Buddha tells him to make offerings, as the rains retreat ends, to the whole community of monks, and the gift given in her name frees her. The puzzle's answer sits in the second half, which is easy to skip.
Moggallana, grateful, asks a question for everyone after him: can people in the future do this for their parents too?
Yes, the Buddha says, and he names both kinds: parents still living, for long life and health, and parents who have died, for release from suffering. So the sutra was never only about the dead.

It's about the people you owe your life to, on both sides of that line. That's the teaching under both festivals: gratitude to parents, and merit given in someone's name, shared with the living and the dead.
The roses aren't in the sutra; they're credited to a short essay by the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh, about wearing a flower for your mother. The lamps and the welcome fires say the other half.

teach.h: THE GONE ARE INVITED, NOT ONLY MOURNED.
teach.b: The ones who are gone are invited, not only mourned.
Obon sets a place for them, and gives in their name.

how: At Obon, Japanese families clean graves, set food and flowers at the home altar, light welcome and farewell fires, and dance the Bon Odori; at Vu Lan, Vietnamese Buddhists give to temples in their parents' names, and at some temples people wear a red or white rose.

o: a Japanese harvest dance with no Buddhist root
a festival welcoming the dead home, from a sutra
a day for chasing ghosts away with loud noise

games.q: one sutra, two festivals — tap the pairs.
p: Japan: fires to welcome the dead home
Vietnam: a rose for your mother

s: the Ullambana Sutra is only about the dead
Moggallana asks for people in the future, and the Buddha names parents living and parents gone.
Obon and Vu Lan grew from the same sutra
both come from the Ullambana Sutra and Moggallana's mother.
the rose custom is written in the sutra
the sutra has no roses; the custom is credited to an essay by Thich Nhat Hanh.

games.q: your friend's family keeps Obon for her late grandfather. her mom, alive and worn out, does all the cooking. by the sutra, who is the festival for?
o: both: the grandfather who's gone and the mom who's still here.
only the grandfather; the living are honored on other days.
only the monks, since the gifts go to the temple.
games.why: Moggallana asked whether others could do this for their parents, and the Buddha named both: parents living, for long life, and parents gone, for release.

practice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp; if not, rest your eyes on any light in the room. For each person you've lost, these five years or long ago, let the flame hold their name for one breath.
When the names run out, keep looking at the light, and let it be a welcome.

wordCard.voice: Obon: the days when the dead are welcomed home with fires and lanterns, from the Ullambana Sutra.

carryVoice: Your line: they come home, and the living get a flower too. Three of seven, lit.

sources.ref: Ullambana Sutra (Moggallana's mother among the hungry ghosts; the offering at the end of the rains; the question for future disciples and their parents, living and dead)
Thich Nhat Hanh, 'A Rose for Your Pocket' (the essay behind the rose custom at Vu Lan)
